s2-bio-01.stem: A nursery owner wants to slow the growth of roots in seedlings that are crowding a small greenhouse and tests compound X. Based on the data and the known action of compound X, which prediction is best supported if the owner applies compound X to all seedlings for several weeks?

stimulus.description: Percentage of root-tip cells in each cell cycle phase for untreated and inhibitor-treated seedlings.

data.title: Root-tip cells by cell cycle phase after 24 h
data.note: Compound X is known to block the activity of cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) complexes that act at the G1/S checkpoint.

options.text: Root growth will be unchanged because cell size, not cell division, determines how much roots grow.
options.why: Misconception: ignores that root growth in the tip depends on cell division; the large shift in phase distribution shows division is affected.

options.text: Root growth will speed up because cells skip the G1/S checkpoint and move quickly into mitosis.
options.why: Misconception: inhibiting a kinase removes the checkpoint and speeds division; in fact CDK activity is required to pass the checkpoint, and M-phase cells fell from 15% to 5%.

options.text: Root growth will slow because cells complete S phase but cannot separate chromosomes during M phase.
options.why: Misconception: places the block at M phase; data show S-phase cells decreased to 5%, so cells are not reaching S and accumulating later, and the M fraction fell because few cells enter the cycle.

options.text: Root growth will slow because cells are held at the G1/S checkpoint and enter S phase less often, so fewer cells divide.
options.why: Correct: CDK inhibition at G1/S increases the G1 fraction (50 to 85%) and drops S and M fractions, so fewer cells divide and root growth slows.

s2-bio-01.explanation_en: Compound X inhibits CDK activity needed to pass the G1/S checkpoint. The table shows G1 cells rising from 50% to 85% while S, G2, and M each fall, meaning cells are arrested before DNA replication and fewer enter division. Fewer divisions in the root tip means slower root growth. The speed-up prediction is wrong because blocking CDK activity prevents, not removes, progression past the checkpoint, and M-phase cells decreased. The M-phase failure prediction is wrong because cells are stalled before S phase (S fell to 5%), not after completing S. The no-change prediction is wrong because the root-tip phase distribution shows division is strongly affected, and root elongation depends on new cells being produced.

s2-bio-02.stem: A sports-medicine team claims that slow-twitch and fast-twitch fibers in the same athlete differ in their myosin proteins because the two fiber types express different subsets of the same genome, not because they contain different genes. Which statement best supports this claim using the data in the table?

stimulus.description: Table of gene copy number per diploid nucleus and relative mRNA level for three genes in slow-twitch and fast-twitch muscle fibers taken from one sprinter's thigh muscle.

data.title: Muscle fibers from one athlete
columns: Relative mRNA level, slow fiber (arbitrary units)
Relative mRNA level, fast fiber (arbitrary units)

options.text: Both fiber types carry two copies of MYH7 and of MYH2, but each fiber type has high mRNA for only one of the two myosin genes.
options.why: Correct: equal gene copy number in both fiber types rules out different genomes, while the mRNA differences show that different genes are transcribed in each fiber type.

options.text: Both fiber types have high ACTB mRNA, which shows that all genes are transcribed at equal levels in every cell of the body.
options.why: Misconception: housekeeping gene expression is generalized to all genes; the table shows MYH7 and MYH2 mRNA levels differ strongly, so expression is not equal.

options.text: Slow fibers have much more MYH7 mRNA than fast fibers, which shows that slow fibers contain extra copies of the MYH7 gene.
options.why: Misconception: higher mRNA is assumed to come from gene amplification; the table shows both fiber types have 2 copies.

options.text: Fast fibers have much more MYH2 mRNA than slow fibers, which shows that slow fibers lost the MYH2 gene during specialization.
options.why: Misconception: specialization is assumed to involve gene loss; the table shows slow fibers still have 2 copies of MYH2.

s2-bio-02.explanation_en: The claim has two parts: the genomes are the same, and the expression differs. The table shows 2 copies of each gene in both fiber types, so the genetic content is the same, while MYH7 mRNA is high only in slow fibers and MYH2 mRNA is high only in fast fibers, so each fiber type expresses a different subset of the genes. The ACTB option is wrong because only a housekeeping gene is equal, and the myosin genes clearly differ, so expression is not equal for all genes. The extra-copies option is wrong because the copy number is 2 in both fiber types, so higher mRNA reflects greater transcription and not more gene copies. The gene-loss option is wrong because slow fibers still carry 2 copies of MYH2, so the gene was not lost; it is expressed at a low level.

s2-bio-03.stem: A family adds lactase drops to milk to make it lactose-free. The table shows the results. Which explanation best accounts for the small increase in glucose when the drops are doubled from 8 to 16?

stimulus.description: Table of glucose produced after 10 minutes in a carton of milk containing 50 mmol lactose at 4 degrees C, for different numbers of lactase drops.

data.title: Lactose hydrolysis in refrigerated milk after 10 minutes
data.conditions: Initial lactose 50 mmol per carton; 4 degrees C; each mole of lactose yields 1 mole glucose and 1 mole galactose; same carton volume in all trials

options.text: The extra lactase molecules are denatured by the cold, so their active sites change shape and cannot bind lactose.
options.why: Misconception: cold denatures enzymes. Cold slows reactions but does not denature, and the lower drop amounts worked at the same temperature.

options.text: Nearly all lactose has already been converted to products at 8 drops, so few substrate molecules remain to bind active sites of the added lactase.
options.why: Correct: 48 of 50 mmol already hydrolyzed, so substrate is limiting; more enzyme cannot make more product.

options.text: Lactase is consumed as it forms enzyme-substrate complexes, so additional drops are used up before they can act.
options.why: Misconception: enzymes are consumed in reactions. Enzymes are recycled and unchanged after catalysis.

options.text: At 16 drops the enzyme lowers the energy released by the reaction, so less glucose is produced overall.
options.why: Misconception: enzymes change the overall energy change or yield of reaction; they lower activation energy only and do not alter total product possible.

s2-bio-03.explanation_en: Glucose rises in proportion to drops from 2 to 8 (12, 24, 48 mmol), showing enzyme amount limits the rate. By 8 drops, 48 of the 50 mmol lactose is already hydrolyzed, so only 2 mmol of substrate remain; 16 drops can produce at most 2 mmol more (observed 50). Thus substrate availability limits product. The cold-denaturation option is wrong because 4 degrees C slows molecular motion without denaturing, and the same temperature allowed proportional activity at lower amounts. The enzyme-consumed option is wrong because enzymes are released unchanged after each reaction and reused. The energy option is wrong because enzymes lower activation energy and do not change the total energy released or the maximum product.

s2-bio-04.stem: A sports-physiology team models growing muscle cells as cubes and calculates the values in the table. They want a graph that represents how cell size affects the cell's capacity to exchange oxygen and wastes with its surroundings per unit of cell volume. Which graph and interpretation best represent the relationship shown in the table?

stimulus.description: Table of modeled cube-shaped cells: side length, surface area, volume, and surface area-to-volume ratio.

data.title: Model muscle cells treated as cubes

options.text: SA/V on the y-axis versus side length on the x-axis, a curve that falls steeply and then levels off, showing that larger cells have less membrane available per unit volume
options.why: Correct: SA/V = 6/side, an inverse relationship; the curve drops steeply then flattens, and less membrane per volume limits exchange in larger cells.

options.text: SA/V on the y-axis versus side length on the x-axis, a straight line rising from the origin, showing that larger cells have more membrane available per unit volume
options.why: Confuses total surface area increasing with size with the ratio; ignores that volume grows faster (cubed) than surface area (squared).

options.text: SA/V on the y-axis versus side length on the x-axis, a straight line falling by the same amount for each doubling, showing that exchange capacity declines at a constant rate
options.why: Treats the decline as linear; the table shows 6, 3, 1.5, 0.75, which halve with each doubling (not equal decreases of constant amount).

options.text: Volume on the y-axis versus surface area on the x-axis, a straight line rising from the origin, showing that exchange capacity per unit volume stays constant as cells grow
options.why: Plots the wrong variables and assumes surface area and volume scale proportionally; volume scales as side cubed and area as side squared, so the ratio is not constant.

s2-bio-04.explanation_en: SA/V equals 6 divided by side length, so each doubling of side length halves the ratio (6, 3, 1.5, 0.75). This is an inverse relationship, giving a curve that drops steeply and then levels off. A smaller SA/V means less membrane per unit of volume for exchange, which limits larger cells. The rising-line option confuses total surface area with the ratio, since volume grows faster than area. The equal-decrease line option is wrong because the drops are 3, 1.5, 0.75 (halving), not constant. The volume-versus-area option is wrong because volume is not proportional to area (cube versus square), so exchange capacity per volume does not stay constant.

s2-bio-05.stem: A research team designed inhibitor Z-41 against human KLR2 and tested it on the KLR2 enzyme from four organisms, as shown in the table. The team now finds a newly sequenced vertebrate whose KLR2 active-site region is 94% identical to human KLR2. Which prediction about Z-41 and the best justification is most consistent with the data and with common ancestry?

stimulus.description: Table of percent amino acid identity between the human version of enzyme KLR2 and the KLR2 enzymes of four organisms, with the measured inhibitor concentration that reduces activity by half for each.

data.title: Comparison of KLR2 active-site region (120 amino acids) with human KLR2
columns: Percent amino acid identity to human KLR2 (%)
Inhibitor concentration giving 50% reduction in activity (nM)
data.note: Inhibitor Z-41 was designed using the structure of human KLR2. Lower values of the 50% reduction concentration mean stronger inhibition.

options.text: Z-41 will inhibit the new enzyme at a concentration near 12-15 nM, because organisms with similar enzymes must have acquired the same mutations independently in response to similar environments.
options.why: Right numerical prediction but wrong reasoning: attributes similarity to independent convergent mutations rather than inheritance from a recent common ancestor.

options.text: Z-41 will inhibit the new enzyme at a concentration near 140 nM, because all vertebrates share a common ancestor and so inhibit the enzyme equally weakly.
options.why: Misconception: shared ancestry alone (being a vertebrate) guarantees an identical response, ignoring that the degree of divergence matters; the data show zebrafish at 62% identity is much weaker, and 94% identity is far above that.

options.text: Z-41 will not inhibit the new enzyme, because only the human enzyme shares the exact active-site structure that Z-41 was designed against.
options.why: Misconception: only the exact target can be inhibited; ignores that conserved sequences inherited from common ancestors keep similar structure, as chimpanzee and mouse data show.

options.text: Z-41 will inhibit the new enzyme at a concentration near 12-15 nM, because higher sequence identity reflects a more recent common ancestor and a more similar active-site structure.
options.why: Correct: 94% identity falls between the 99% and 88% organisms, which both show strong inhibition (12 and 15 nM); greater similarity from a more recent common ancestor predicts a conserved active-site structure and similar inhibitor binding.

s2-bio-05.explanation_en: Sequence similarity in conserved proteins reflects how recently species shared a common ancestor: fewer substitutions have accumulated, so the active-site structure is better preserved. In the table, the 99% and 88% identity enzymes are inhibited at 12 and 15 nM, while 62% identity requires 140 nM and 31% identity shows no inhibition. A 94% identical enzyme lies between the two strongly inhibited organisms, so Z-41 should work at roughly 12-15 nM. The option predicting about 140 nM wrongly treats all vertebrates as equally related and ignores the trend with identity. The option predicting no inhibition ignores that conserved structure is inherited, as shown by the chimpanzee and mouse results. The option invoking independent mutations in similar environments gives the right number but a wrong cause, since the similarity is explained by inheritance from a common ancestor, not independent convergence.

s2-bio-06.stem: A family is choosing a grow-light for a basement basil garden. They already own a green LED bulb and test it against red and blue LED bulbs of equal photon flux using leaf discs, with the results shown in the table. Which claim about their purchase is best supported by the data?

stimulus.description: Table of mean net O2 release by basil leaf discs under three LED colors at equal photon flux, plus a dark control, with 2SE values.

data.title: Net O2 exchange of basil leaf discs after 20 min under LED bulbs of equal photon flux (100 umol photons per m^2 per s)
columns: Mean net O2 release (umol O2 per m^2 per s)
data.notes: Negative value means net O2 uptake. n = 10 leaf discs per treatment. Error values are plus or minus 2 SE of the mean.

options.text: Buy a red or blue bulb instead of the green one, because net O2 release was higher under red and blue than under green, and the red and blue values were not clearly different from each other.
options.why: Correct: red (8.4 +/- 0.6) and blue (7.9 +/- 0.5) intervals overlap, and both are far above green (3.1 +/- 0.4), so red/blue support more photosynthesis than green at equal photon flux.

options.text: Buy the red bulb only, because its mean net O2 release was higher than that of the blue bulb, showing red is the most effective wavelength for basil.
options.why: Misconception: treating any difference in means as a real difference while ignoring overlapping 2SE intervals (7.8-9.0 vs 7.4-8.4).

options.text: Keep the green bulb, because basil leaves reflect green light, showing that green light is used efficiently without wasting energy.
options.why: Misconception: believing reflected wavelengths are the most efficiently used; reflection means less absorption, and the data show lower O2 output under green.

options.text: Keep the green bulb as the only light source, because net O2 release under green light was low, showing the leaf discs carried out no photosynthesis.
options.why: Misconception: equating low net O2 with zero photosynthesis; net 3.1 is above zero and gross is about 4.3 after adding respiration (1.2), and the recommendation also conflicts with the lower output.

s2-bio-06.explanation_en: Net O2 release under red (8.4 +/- 0.6) and blue (7.9 +/- 0.5) is well above that under green (3.1 +/- 0.4), with non-overlapping intervals, so red or blue light supports more photosynthesis at equal photon flux. The red and blue intervals overlap, so the data do not show that one is better than the other; recommending red only is unsupported. Recommending the green bulb because leaves reflect green reverses the logic: reflected light is not absorbed, and the measured O2 output is lowest under green. Saying green drives no photosynthesis is wrong because net O2 release is positive (3.1), and gross production is about 4.3 once dark respiration (1.2) is added back; the choice to keep green as the only light also ignores the better-performing bulbs.

s2-bio-07.stem: The table shows the relative rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction at different pH values. A researcher raises the pH of a mixture from 5 to 6, keeping temperature, enzyme amount, and saturating substrate unchanged. Which prediction about the rate, and its cause, is best supported by the data?

stimulus.description: Relative rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction at six pH values, 25 C, saturating substrate.

data.conditions: 25 C, substrate concentration saturating, same enzyme amount in every trial

options.text: The rate will decrease, because any increase in pH moves the enzyme farther from its optimum and begins denaturing the protein.
options.why: Misconception: higher pH is always harmful or denaturing; the data show the rate rises toward the optimum at pH 7, so pH 6 is closer to the optimum than pH 5.

options.text: The rate will increase about 2.8-fold, because the higher pH supplies additional substrate molecules that raise the frequency of enzyme-substrate collisions.
options.why: Misconception: pH changes the amount of substrate; substrate is stated to be saturating and unchanged, so collision frequency is not the cause.

options.text: The rate will stay about the same, because the enzyme is already saturated with substrate and a pH change cannot alter a saturated enzyme.
options.why: Misconception: saturation makes the rate independent of all conditions; saturation removes substrate limitation but pH still changes the catalytic efficiency of each enzyme.

options.text: The rate will increase about 2.8-fold, because the pH change moves ionizable active-site groups closer to the charge state needed for substrate binding and catalysis.
options.why: Correct: 61/22 is about 2.8, and pH affects the ionization of active-site and substrate-binding groups, changing activity.

s2-bio-07.explanation_en: The data show the rate rising from 22 at pH 5 to 61 at pH 6, about a 2.8-fold increase, as pH approaches the optimum of 7. Changing pH alters the ionization of amino acid side chains in the active site, which affects substrate binding and catalysis, so the key is correct. The substrate-supply explanation fails because substrate is saturating and unchanged, so pH is not adding substrate. The no-change prediction fails because saturation only means substrate is not limiting; the activity of each enzyme molecule still depends on pH, and the table shows a large change. The decrease prediction fails because the data show the rate is lower at pH 5 than at pH 6, so moving toward the optimum raises the rate; denaturation is not what occurs in this small shift.

s2-bio-08.stem: A sports-science team housed genetically identical mice in two conditions and measured resting heart rate after 8 weeks, as shown in the table. Which statement best explains the difference between the groups?

stimulus.description: Table of mean resting heart rate (beats per minute) for two groups of genetically identical laboratory mice (an inbred strain) after 8 weeks under two housing conditions.

data.title: Mean resting heart rate of inbred mice after 8 weeks
columns: Mean resting heart rate (beats per minute)
data.notes: All mice are genetically identical, same age and sex, same diet and temperature.

options.text: The running-wheel environment influenced expression of the same genotype, producing a different resting heart rate phenotype.
options.why: Correct: with genotype held constant, the environmental difference accounts for the phenotypic difference (phenotype = genotype x environment).

options.text: Exercise caused a mutation in cardiac muscle genes of the running-wheel mice, changing their DNA sequence and lowering heart rate.
options.why: Misconception: environmental factors like exercise cause heritable DNA mutations; the data show no DNA change and training effects are not mutations.

options.text: The groups must differ genetically, because identical genotypes always produce identical phenotypes regardless of environment.
options.why: Misconception: genotype alone fixes phenotype; ignores that the mice are stated to be genetically identical.

options.text: The difference is due to chance alone, because a phenotype is determined only by genotype and cannot be altered by the environment.
options.why: Misconception: phenotype is purely genetic; the difference (55 bpm, several SDs) is too large to attribute to chance and environment does affect phenotype.

s2-bio-08.explanation_en: The mice are genetically identical and differ only in housing, yet their mean heart rates differ by 55 bpm, far more than the standard deviations of about 11-12 bpm. This shows that environment (exercise) altered the phenotype produced by the same genotype. The mutation option is wrong because exercise does not change the DNA sequence and nothing in the data indicates that. The option claiming the groups must differ genetically contradicts the stated identical genotypes and the fact that environment affects phenotype. The chance-only option is wrong because the difference is large relative to the variation, and phenotype depends on both genotype and environment.

s2-bio-09.stem: A researcher adds a drug that specifically blocks the activity of the cyclin E-CDK2 complex, which is required for cells to pass the G1/S checkpoint. The drug is not toxic and does not cause cell death. After 24 hours, which distribution of cells is the most likely result?

stimulus.description: Percent of cultured fibroblasts in each cell-cycle stage in an untreated asynchronous culture, determined by DNA-content flow cytometry.

options.why: Misconception: assumes blocking a G1/S regulator arrests cells in G2/M, confusing which checkpoint the complex controls.
Correct: with cyclin E-CDK2 blocked, cells already past G1/S finish S, G2 and M and divide, but cells in G1 cannot enter S, so cells accumulate in G1 and S and G2+M fractions shrink.
Misconception: assumes the drug has no effect on the distribution, or that the cycle is not regulated by cyclin-CDK activity.
Misconception: assumes that inhibiting the G1/S kinase causes cells to pile up in S phase, treating the inhibitor as a block of DNA replication rather than of entry into S.

s2-bio-09.explanation_en: Cyclin E-CDK2 activity is needed to pass the G1/S checkpoint. When it is blocked, cells already in S, G2 or M continue through the cycle and divide into G1 cells, but no G1 cells can enter S. Over 24 hours the culture therefore shifts strongly toward G1, with S and G2+M fractions falling, which matches the distribution with a large G1 majority. The distribution with mostly G2+M is wrong because the block is at G1/S, not at the G2/M transition. The unchanged distribution is wrong because blocking a required regulator must change the proportions. The distribution with an S-phase majority is wrong because cells cannot enter S without this complex, so S cannot grow.

s2-bio-10.stem: In the control trial, core temperature rise slows as sweat rate increases. Based on the feedback relationship shown, which prediction is best for the second trial, in which the runner's sweat glands cannot respond to nerve signals?

stimulus.description: Table of core body temperature and sweat rate at four time points during a 40-minute treadmill run in a control trial.

data.title: Control trial: treadmill run at constant speed in a 25 C room
data.note: Sweating lowers body temperature by evaporative cooling. In a second trial, the same runner takes a drug that blocks the response of sweat glands to nerve signals; all other conditions are identical.

options.text: Core temperature will rise at the same rate as in the control trial, because the brain's detection of temperature change is unchanged.
options.why: Misconception: assumes that because the sensor is intact the outcome is unchanged, ignoring that the effector is needed to correct the change.

options.text: Core temperature will stay near 37.0 C, because blocking the sweat glands removes the stimulus that raises body temperature.
options.why: Misconception: believes the effector causes the disturbance, confusing the response with the stimulus; exercise heat production continues regardless.

options.text: Core temperature will keep rising faster than in the control trial, because the response that lowers temperature is lost and the rise is no longer opposed.
options.why: Correct: sweating is the effector of a negative feedback loop; blocking it removes opposition to the heat gain, so temperature rises faster.

options.text: Core temperature will fall below 37.0 C, because the blocked glands will trigger an opposing response that overcools the body.
options.why: Misconception: thinks interrupting negative feedback produces an overcorrection in the opposite direction; no cooling mechanism is activated.

s2-bio-10.explanation_en: Sweating is the effector in a negative feedback loop: rising core temperature increases sweat rate, and evaporative cooling opposes the rise, so the control data show the rise slowing (0.6 C in the first 10 min, then 0.3, then 0.1). If the glands cannot respond, the heat produced by exercise is no longer opposed, so temperature should rise faster than in the control trial. The prediction that temperature stays near 37.0 C is wrong because exercise still generates heat; sweating removes heat, it does not cause it. The prediction of an unchanged rate is wrong because intact sensing does not help if the effector cannot act. The prediction of falling below 37.0 C is wrong because blocking a cooling response cannot cause cooling or overcorrection.

s2-bio-11.title: Muscle pH and Enzyme Activity During Sprint Training

stimulus.description: {"kind":"graph","description":"Line graph of relative activity of a muscle enzyme (percent of maximum) versus pH of the surrounding fluid, measured at 37 degrees C. Activity rises from low values at acidic pH to a peak near pH 7.0 and falls at lower and higher pH. Resting muscle pH (7.0) and pH after an all-out sprint (6.4) are marked with vertical dashed lines.","data":{"graph_type":"line with markers","x_axis":{"label":"pH of muscle fluid","min":5.0,"max":8.0,"major_tick":0.5,"units":"pH units"},"y_axis":{"label":"Relative enzyme activity (% of maximum)","min":0,"max":100,"major_tick":20,"units":"%"},"series":[{"legend":"Enzyme X at 37 C","points":[[5.0,5],[5.5,20],[6.0,55],[6.4,80],[6.5,86],[7.0,100],[7.5,70],[8.0,25]]}],"vertical_markers":[{"x":7.0,"label":"Resting muscle"},{"x":6.4,"label":"After all-out sprint"}],"context":"Intense sprinting produces lactic acid, lowering muscle fluid pH. Enzyme X is a muscle enzyme that catalyzes one step of ATP production."}

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how the relative activity of enzyme X changes as pH decreases from 7.0 to 5.0.
parts.model_answer: Activity decreases as pH falls below 7.0, from 100% at pH 7.0 to about 5% at pH 5.0 (a steady decline).

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes decrease in activity with decreasing pH below the optimum, using the graph data
required_elements: activity decreases as pH decreases from 7.0 to 5.0
cites values or the direction from about 100% to about 5%
alt_solutions: Activity is highest at 7.0 and lower at every more acidic pH
common_errors: Says activity increases in acidic conditions
Describes only the pH 7.0 to 8.0 side

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the graph, determine the percentage decrease in activity of enzyme X in muscle immediately after an all-out sprint (pH 6.4) compared with resting muscle (pH 7.0).
parts.model_answer: At pH 6.4 activity is 80% of max versus 100% at rest: (100-80)/100 = 20% decrease (answers 19-21% accepted if graph read as 79-81%).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct percent decrease with values read from graph
required_elements: 80% at pH 6.4 and 100% at pH 7.0
result of 20% decrease
alt_solutions: Activity is 0.8 of resting activity, so 20% lower
common_errors: Reports 20 percentage points without noting it is also 20%

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain, at the level of enzyme structure, why the activity of enzyme X is lower at pH 5.0 than at pH 7.0.
parts.model_answer: Excess H+ at low pH changes the ionization of R groups (amino acids) in the enzyme, disrupting hydrogen/ionic bonds that maintain its 3-D shape. The active site shape changes (denaturation), so substrate binds poorly and fewer reactions are catalyzed.

rubric_rows.criterion: Links pH to altered bonding/R-group charges, changed active site shape, and reduced substrate binding
required_elements: pH change alters R-group charge or ionic/hydrogen bonds
enzyme tertiary structure or active site shape changes
substrate binds less effectively so lower activity
common_errors: Says the enzyme is used up

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A trainer proposes a supplement that raises muscle pH after sprints by 0.5 units (for example, from 6.4 to 6.9). Predict the effect on enzyme X activity and justify your prediction using the graph.
parts.model_answer: Activity would increase, from about 80% to about 98-100% of maximum, because pH 6.9 is close to the optimum of 7.0 where the active site has its best shape for substrate binding.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts increased activity and justifies with graph values near optimum
required_elements: predicts activity increase
justification cites graph (about 80% rising to near 100%) or proximity to pH 7.0 optimum
alt_solutions: Activity would be close to maximum, about 95-100%
common_errors: Predicts decrease because higher pH is always worse

s2-bio-12.title: Inducer-Dependent Reporter Expression in Regulatory Mutants

stimulus.description: Table of mean relative reporter units (RU) with ±2SE for four bacterial strains grown without and with an inducer molecule.

data.units: RU = relative units of reporter protein per cell, measured after 3 h of growth
data.setup: A reporter gene is placed downstream of a promoter and an adjacent operator sequence. A separate gene encodes a repressor protein that binds the operator and blocks transcription. The inducer binds the repressor. Strain R-s makes a repressor that still binds the operator but cannot bind the inducer. All strains carry the same reporter gene and promoter. Cultures were grown in the same medium at the same temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the dependent variable in this experiment, and identify which strain-condition combination serves as the baseline (control) for judging the effect of the inducer on a normally regulated gene. Explain why it is the appropriate control.
parts.model_answer: The dependent variable is reporter expression (RU of reporter protein per cell). The control is the wild-type strain without inducer (or WT with vs. without inducer), because it has an intact repressor and operator and shows the normal regulated (repressed) state against which the mutants and the inducer effect are compared.

required_elements: reporter expression / reporter protein level (RU)
common_errors: Naming the inducer or strain as the dependent variable

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the control and justifies it
required_elements: wild type (with or without inducer)
has intact/functional repressor and operator, so normal regulation is the comparison
alt_solutions: WT without inducer as the uninduced baseline, with WT plus inducer as the induced comparison
common_errors: Choosing a mutant strain as the control

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the table. Describe the graph you would draw: the type of graph, what is plotted on each axis, how the conditions are distinguished, and how the error bars are shown.
parts.model_answer: Draw a grouped (clustered) bar graph. The x-axis lists the four strains (WT, R-, O-c, R-s), each with two adjacent bars (no inducer, inducer added) distinguished by shading and a legend. The y-axis is mean reporter expression (RU), scaled 0 to about 110 with even intervals. Bar heights equal the means (2.0/96.0, 91.0/94.0, 88.0/90.0, 1.8/2.4), with error bars of +/-2SE (0.6, 8.0, 7.0, 9.0, 8.0, 7.0, 0.5, 0.7).

required_elements: bar graph with paired/grouped bars by strain and condition (categorical x-axis)
alt_solutions: Separate bar graphs for each condition, with strains on the x-axis

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted data with error bars
required_elements: bar heights match the means for all eight bars
error bars of +/-2SE drawn on each bar
common_errors: Using SE values as bar heights

required_elements: y-axis labeled reporter expression (RU) with a uniform scale
x-axis labeled strain
legend or key identifying no inducer vs. inducer added

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold induction (expression with inducer divided by expression without inducer) for the wild-type strain. Show your work.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct fold induction with work shown
required_elements: answer of 48

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student claims: 'The O-c mutation changes the operator so that the repressor can no longer block transcription, whereas the R-s mutation changes the repressor so that it cannot respond to the inducer.' Use the data to support this claim, and explain how each mutation produces its pattern. Then predict the reporter expression (high or low) without inducer in a strain that carries both the wild-type repressor gene and the O-c operator, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: Evidence for O-c: expression is high (88.0 RU) even without inducer and is similar to the repressor deletion (91.0 RU), with overlapping error bars with inducer (90.0 RU), so the gene is expressed constitutively; an altered operator sequence prevents repressor binding, so RNA polymerase can transcribe regardless of the inducer. Evidence for R-s: expression stays low with and without inducer (1.8 and 2.4 RU, overlapping error bars), so the repressor keeps blocking transcription because it cannot bind the inducer and so is never released from the operator. Prediction: high expression without inducer, because the wild-type repressor is present but the mutated operator cannot bind it, so transcription is not blocked.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses O-c data (with numbers) to support constitutive expression and links to altered operator preventing repressor binding
required_elements: O-c high without inducer (about 88 RU), similar to R- and not increased by inducer
mutated operator cannot bind repressor so transcription is not blocked
common_errors: Claiming the O-c mutation removes the repressor protein

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses R-s data (with numbers) to support lack of induction and links to repressor unable to bind inducer
required_elements: R-s low with and without inducer (about 2 RU), overlapping error bars
repressor cannot bind inducer so remains bound to operator and keeps blocking transcription
high expression without inducer
operator cannot bind the repressor even though repressor is present (cis-acting site mutation)

s2-bio-13.stem: A circular plasmid of 4,200 bp was digested with one restriction enzyme, and the products were separated by gel electrophoresis alongside size standards. The gel data are shown. Which conclusion about the enzyme and the plasmid is best supported by the data?

stimulus.description: Ladder fragment sizes with migration distances, and two bands from a digest of a 4,200 bp circular plasmid.

data.gel_notes: Agarose gel; distance measured in mm from the well toward the positive electrode. For these standards, migration distance is a straight-line function of log10(fragment size in bp).

options.text: The enzyme cuts the plasmid at one site; two bands appear because the two DNA strands separate during the run.
options.why: Misconception: double-stranded DNA separates into strands in a native agarose gel and gives extra bands; it does not, and one cut would give a single 4,200 bp linear band.

options.text: The enzyme cuts the plasmid at two sites; band sizes of about 3,150 bp and 1,000 bp sum to roughly the plasmid size.
options.why: Correct: the log-linear standard curve gives about 3,150 and 1,000 bp; these sum to about 4,150 bp, matching the 4,200 bp circle, and a circular plasmid yields two fragments only if cut twice.

options.text: The enzyme cuts the plasmid at two sites; band sizes of about 4,100 bp and 1,850 bp sum to roughly the plasmid size.
options.why: Misconception: treating distance as linear in size rather than in log size gives wrong sizes; they sum to about 5,950 bp, more than the plasmid.

options.text: The enzyme cuts the plasmid at one site; the smaller band is a partial digestion product that is not part of the plasmid.
options.why: Misconception: explains away data that contradict the claim; one cut in a circle gives one band, and the two bands sum to the plasmid size so both come from it.

s2-bio-13.explanation_en: Distance is linear in log10(size). Using the two standards, the slope is -20 mm per tenfold change in size. Band at 26 mm is about 1,000 bp and band at 16 mm is about 3,150 bp. Their sum, about 4,150 bp, matches the 4,200 bp plasmid, so all of the DNA is accounted for by two fragments. A circular molecule cut once gives one linear fragment, and cut twice gives two, so the enzyme cuts at two sites. The strand-separation option is wrong because native gels do not separate strands, and one cut would give a single band. The linear-interpolation option is wrong because it ignores the log relationship, and its sizes sum to about 5,950 bp, which exceeds the plasmid size. The partial-digest option is wrong because the two bands together account for the whole plasmid, so the smaller band is part of it, and one cut would not give two plasmid fragments.
